value.text: Four travellers must cross a bridge at night with one torch. At most two cross at a time and a pair moves at the slower person's pace. They take 1, 2, 5 and 10 minutes. What is the fastest total crossing time, and what is the schedule?

This is the classic bridge and torch puzzle with crossing times of 1, 2, 5, and 10 minutes, and I recall the optimal solution takes 17 minutes. I'm working out the sequence: send 1 and 2 across together, have 1 return, send 5 and 10 across together, have 2 return, then finish with 1 and 2 crossing again.

Now I'm checking why this beats the naive strategy of just shuttling the fastest person back and forth, which costs 19 minutes instead. The key insight is pairing the two slowest people together on one trip rather than making the fastest person escort them separately, and I'm trying to formalize why five crossings is the minimum needed and why 17 is truly optimal.

Someone must bring the torch back after 5 and 10 cross; if they go first, the return costs at least 5. If instead 1 and 2 go first (cost 2) and one returns (cost 1), then 5 and 10 cross (cost 10), someone must still return — minimizing that return cost matters for the total.

Trying F1={5,10} cost 10, R1=5 cost 5, then F2={1,2} cost 2 but 5 still needs to get back across eventually with someone, pushing the total well past 17.

Testing F2={5,10} instead: F1={1,2} cost 2, R1 brings one of them back (cost ≥1), then F2={5,10} costs 10, R2 sends back the cheaper person left on the far side, F3={1,2} cost 2 — this path totals exactly 17.

I notice there are actually two distinct optimal schedules depending on whether 1 or 2 does the first return trip, both summing to 17. Now I'm checking the case where 5 and 10 cross on separate trips, which forces the forward costs higher since the third forward trip still needs at least one more crossing.

Working through this: forward trips alone cost at least 10+5+1=16, plus at least two return trips at minimum 1 each, pushing the total to 18, which exceeds 17 and confirms that case is worse.

Now I'm checking Case A, where 5 and 10 cross together. If that pairing happens last, I need the earlier four crossings (two forward, two back) using just 1 and 2 to have shuffled things correctly, so I'm tracing through whether that sequence actually works.

But that creates a contradiction, since whoever carried the torch back to the start would then be stuck there after F3, unless they're part of that final crossing — meaning the last trip can't cleanly be just 5 and 10 alone.

So I'm checking if {5,10} works as the first trip instead, with 5 or 10 as the returner, which pushes the total cost up near 18 or more.

With more than three forward trips, I need a cleaner bound: more crossings generally mean higher cost, so I'm trying to pin down whether four forward trips could still stay at 17 or less.

Thinking it through, 5 and 10 each need to cross forward at least once, and if they never pair up for other trips, every remaining crossing is handled solely by 1 and 2 shuttling back and forth, so I'm tallying up those shuttle costs.

This confirms the known minimum of 17 minutes, with the two slowest crossing together while 1 and 2 handle the torch returns. I want to double-check this via a mental BFS to be fully confident 17 is optimal.

Computing option 2 numerically gives 1+2+2+2+10=17, which beats option 1's 19, so the optimal crossing time is 17 minutes. I want to double-check this against a full state-space search before finalizing.

I want to double-check this rigorously. If 5 and 10 never travel together on any forward trip, their crossing costs are separate and at least 15 combined, plus the structure requires at least three forward trips and two return trips, which pushes the total toward the 17 lower bound.

If 5 and 10 do travel together once, that trip costs 10, and I need to account for all other trips—likely involving just 1 and 2—to see whether the remaining cost can still reach 17 or more.

So before the 5-10 crossing, there must be at least one forward trip and one return trip involving 1 and/or 2, bringing the torch back to the start. Checking whether both 1 and 2 could already be on the far side at that point leads to a contradiction, since the last return trip would require the returner to be at the start side, so at least one of 1 or 2 must still be at the start when the 5-10 trip begins.

After the 5-10 trip, that remaining person is stuck at the start with the torch gone to the far side, forcing a second return trip and a third forward trip to finally get everyone across — giving a minimum structure of five trips total: F1, R1, the 5-10 crossing, R2, and F3, with costs adding up based on who makes each return.

Checking total cost: 2 + x + 10 + y + 2 = 14 + x + y, and with x,y being 1 and 2, that's 14 + 3 = 17. I'm also verifying that any configuration using more than 5 trips (like 7 total trips) can't beat this, since each extra forward/return pair by 1 and 2 only adds cost without reducing the fixed 10-cost crossing.

So the total meets at least 17 even with 7 trips, and extending to more trips only increases the lower bound further since each additional round adds more forward and return costs.

The minimum is 17 minutes. I'll lay out the schedule: 1&2 cross (2 min, total 2), 1 returns (1 min, total 3), 5&10 cross (10 min, total 13), then 2 returns (2 min, total 15), and 1&2 cross again (2 min, total 17).

The reasoning for why we can't do better: the 10 must cross once, costing 10 minutes minimum, and sending 5 separately would add another 5, pushing the total past 18 — so 5 and 10 need to cross together in one trip, with a fast person positioned to shuttle the torch back and forth. There's also an alternate 17-minute schedule where 2 returns before 1 does, and I should note that the "1 escorts everyone" approach only reaches 19 minutes, which is worse.

**The fastest total time is 17 minutes.**

**Schedule**

| Step | Action | Time | Running total |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 and 2 cross together | 2 | 2 |
| 2 | 1 walks back with the torch | 1 | 3 |
| 3 | 5 and 10 cross together | 10 | 13 |
| 4 | 2 walks back with the torch | 2 | 15 |
| 5 | 1 and 2 cross together | 2 | 17 |

(Swapping who returns also works: 1 and 2 cross, 2 returns, 5 and 10 cross, 1 returns, 1 and 2 cross. That is 2+2+10+1+2 = 17 as well.)

**Why nothing is faster**

- The obvious plan is to let the 1-minute person escort everyone. That takes 2+1+5+1+10 = 19 minutes.
- Any schedule needs at least 5 crossings: 3 forward and 2 back.
- If 5 and 10 cross in separate trips, those two trips alone cost 15. The other three crossings cost at least 1 each, so the total is at least 18.
- So 5 and 10 should cross together, paying for the 10-minute walk only once. The torch must then already be on the far side with someone fast, and must be brought back afterwards by another fast person. That is exactly what the 1 and 2 do, and it gives 17.
